analysis.one_liner: Orders the federal commodity regulator to impose strict trading limits on banks and hedge funds in energy markets.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the agency policing futures markets, to use its emergency powers to curb excessive speculation in energy markets. It would have immediately classified banks trading energy futures as speculators subject to strict position limits, required hedge funds trading energy futures to register and obey speculation limits, broken up conflicts where one firm forecasts oil prices, operates oil infrastructure, and trades oil derivatives, and revoked exemptions that let foreign exchanges trade U.S. energy contracts to U.S. investors from terminals in this country. Its sponsors pointed to gas prices rising from $1.64 to over $2.61 a gallon while U.S. oil demand and inventories pointed the other way.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially drivers and households paying gasoline, heating oil, and electricity bills that follow crude oil prices. Businesses that buy fuel, like airlines and trucking companies, would also benefit if the limits reduced price swings. Honest energy producers and end users would gain from prices that reflect actual supply and demand rather than speculative trading.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and households paying energy bills

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the CFTC to use its existing emergency authority to eliminate excessive speculation and price distortion in energy futures and swaps markets, so prices reflect supply and demand rather than speculative positions [S2].

It would have immediately subjected bank holding companies trading energy futures to strict position limits by classifying them as noncommercial speculators, ending their treatment as ordinary hedgers [S2].
It required hedge funds trading energy futures to register with the CFTC and obey strict speculation limits, bringing a lightly regulated class of traders under oversight [S2].

It directed the CFTC to eliminate conflicts of interest where a single entity predicts oil prices, operates oil assets like pipelines and storage, and trades energy derivatives, and to revoke staff no-action letters letting foreign exchanges trade U.S. commodities to U.S. investors from terminals in the United States [S2].

The bill's findings noted gas prices jumped from $1.64 to over $2.61 a gallon between December 2008 and June 2009 while U.S. oil inventories hit record highs and demand fell to a decade low, the pattern that motivated the crackdown [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks with energy trading desks, hedge funds, and foreign exchanges with U.S. terminals would lose speculative profits and trading volume. Traders on the losing side of unwound or limited positions could absorb losses, and reduced speculative trading could mean somewhat less liquidity in energy futures markets, which some argue raises hedging costs for legitimate users.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, hedge funds, and energy traders

drawbacks.text: Economists disagree about how much speculation drives oil prices; the bill's own findings could also be read as evidence that factors other than speculative volume were lifting prices, so strict limits might not lower pump prices [S3].

Position limits and forced reclassification reduce trading volume and liquidity, which can raise hedging costs for legitimate users of futures markets such as airlines and refiners, a cost honest supporters would have to acknowledge.
Restricting U.S. trading could push some energy speculation to venues outside CFTC jurisdiction, limiting the practical effect unless foreign regulators acted in step.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If speculation was distorting energy prices as the findings claimed, the consumer benefit from stable, supply-and-demand-based prices would be broad and immediate, while the costs would fall on a narrow set of financial traders. The main uncertainty is effectiveness: whether position limits would actually reduce prices, and whether restrictions would simply move trading offshore. The bill's blunt mandates ('immediately' classify, revoke, and curb) traded precision for speed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Energy Market Manipulation Prevention Act on June 10, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
No further action was ever taken on the bill; it sat in committee until the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].
Only two senators, both Democrats, cosponsored the bill alongside its Independent sponsor [S4].

The bill would have required the CFTC to impose strict position limits on banks and hedge funds trading energy futures, eliminate conflicts of interest among firms that forecast, move, and trade oil, and revoke exemptions for foreign exchanges with U.S. trading terminals [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, hedge funds, and other financial firms trading energy futures kept operating under the pre-crisis rules, with no strict position limits and no forced registration, since the bill never advanced. Consumers kept bearing whatever effect speculative trading had on energy prices.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks urging the CFTC to curb energy market speculation

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never reported it out, held no hearing or markup, and never scheduled it for a vote

against.name: Blanche Lincoln
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for committee action during her tenure

against.name: Large banks and hedge funds trading energy futures
against.role: Financial firms that would face strict position limits and registration
against.what_they_did: Opposed strict position limits on energy derivatives trading during this period

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only recorded support was the Independent sponsor and 2 Democratic cosponsors out of 58 Senate Democrats, and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have immediately reclassified every bank holding company trading energy futures as a noncommercial speculator subject to strict position limits, capping the size of their energy bets and the profits that go with them. Consumers pay energy prices these trading activities can inflate.

Hedge funds trading energy futures would have had to register with the CFTC and obey strict speculation limits, reducing a lightly regulated profit center. Their gains come from the same price swings households pay at the pump.

industries.industry: Foreign exchanges with U.S. trading terminals
industries.note: The bill would have revoked staff no-action letters letting foreign boards of trade trade U.S. commodities to U.S. investors from terminals in the United States, closing a channel for unlimited speculation outside U.S. limits.

industries.industry: Firms that own oil infrastructure and trade energy derivatives
industries.note: The bill targeted conflicts where one entity forecasts oil prices, operates pipelines and storage, and trades energy derivatives, giving such firms inside knowledge of the markets they trade. Breaking that up costs them an informational edge.

industries.industry: Airlines, truckers, and other fuel buyers who hedge
industries.note: These businesses rely on futures markets to lock in fuel costs; position limits could modestly raise their hedging costs if liquidity thins, but prices that reflect real supply and demand would make their fuel costs more predictable.
